meta.title: OCR Y544 Discrete Mathematics
meta.notes: Question content for the Y544 revision app. See README.md for the full schema. All four top-level mode keys are required; each holds an array of items (pivot holds presets plus a generator flag).

quickfire.prompt: How many edges does the complete graph K6 have?
quickfire.explanation: Kn has n(n−1)/2 edges, so K6 has 6×5/2 = 15.

quickfire.prompt: A connected graph is Eulerian if and only if…
options: it has exactly two vertices of odd degree
quickfire.explanation: Eulerian = closed trail using every arc exactly once, which requires every vertex to have even degree. Exactly two odd vertices gives a semi-Eulerian graph.

quickfire.prompt: In the simplex algorithm, the pivot row is chosen using…
options: the largest ratio of RHS ÷ pivot-column entry
the most negative entry in the objective row
the smallest non-negative ratio of RHS ÷ positive pivot-column entry
the row with the largest RHS value
quickfire.explanation: The ratio test: divide RHS by the pivot-column entry for rows where that entry is positive, and choose the smallest non-negative ratio. The most negative objective entry chooses the pivot COLUMN.

quickfire.prompt: Euler's formula for a connected planar graph states…
quickfire.explanation: Vertices − Edges + Faces = 2. To 'verify' it in an exam you must substitute the actual values of V, E and F, not just quote it.
Bubble (and shuttle) sort are O(n²) in the worst case; quick sort averages O(n log n). For O(n²), doubling the list size roughly quadruples the run time.

ordering.title: Simplex: one complete iteration
steps: Choose the pivot column: the column with the most negative entry in the objective row.
For each row with a positive entry in the pivot column, calculate RHS ÷ pivot-column entry.
Choose the pivot row: the row with the smallest non-negative ratio.
Divide every entry in the pivot row by the pivot element.
Add or subtract multiples of the pivot row so every other entry in the pivot column becomes 0.
If the objective row still has a negative entry, repeat; otherwise the solution is optimal.

ordering.title: Simplex: setting up the initial tableau
steps: Write the problem in standard form: maximise P subject to ≤ constraints and non-negative variables.
Introduce a slack variable into each constraint to turn it into an equation.
Rearrange the objective so that P minus the objective expression equals 0.
Enter the constraint equations as the body rows of the tableau.
Enter the objective equation as the bottom row, giving negative coefficients for the variables.

ordering.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
steps: Give the start vertex the permanent label 0, with order of labelling 1.
Update the temporary labels at every vertex directly connected to the vertex just made permanent, if the new value is smaller.
Make the smallest temporary label permanent, recording its order of labelling.
Repeat updating and selecting until the destination vertex receives a permanent label.
Trace back from the destination, using arcs where the difference in permanent labels equals the arc weight, to find the route.

ordering.title: Route inspection (closed route)
steps: Find the degree of each vertex and list the vertices of odd degree.
List every way the odd vertices can be paired up.
Find the total of the shortest paths for each complete pairing.
Choose the pairing with the smallest total and repeat those paths in the network.
Add the smallest pairing total to the total weight of all the arcs to obtain the route length.

ordering.title: Route inspection (start and finish at different vertices)
steps: Find the vertices of odd degree.
Note that with different start and finish vertices, exactly two odd vertices may be left unpaired.
For each choice of the two vertices left unpaired, find the shortest-path total needed to pair up the remaining odd vertices.
Choose the option with the smallest repeated total, which also identifies the best start and finish vertices.
Add the repeated total to the total weight of all the arcs.

spotTheError.prompt: A network has total arc weight 84. Find the length of the shortest closed route covering every arc. The shortest paths between odd vertices are BD = 7, EG = 9, BE = 6, DG = 8, BG = 11, DE = 5.
lines: The odd vertices are B, D, E and G.
Possible pairings: BD + EG = 7 + 9 = 16; BE + DG = 6 + 8 = 14; BG + DE = 11 + 5 = 16.
Choose the pairing BD + EG = 16 as the paths to repeat.
Shortest route = 84 + 16 = 100.
spotTheError.explanation: You must repeat the pairing with the SMALLEST total, which is BE + DG = 14, not 16. The shortest route is 84 + 14 = 98.

spotTheError.prompt: An iteration of the simplex algorithm uses pivot column y. The y-column entries in the three constraint rows are 2, −1 and 4, with RHS values 10, 8 and 12.
lines: The pivot column is y, since −7 is the most negative entry in the objective row.
Ratio test: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, 8 ÷ (−1) = −8 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so the second row (smallest ratio, −8) is the pivot row.
Divide the pivot row by the pivot element.
Add or subtract multiples of the pivot row so the other pivot-column entries become 0.
spotTheError.explanation: The ratio test only uses rows whose pivot-column entry is POSITIVE, so the row with entry −1 is excluded entirely. The valid ratios are 5 and 3, and the smallest is 3, so the third row is the pivot row.

spotTheError.prompt: Use the nearest neighbour algorithm starting at A to find an upper bound for the travelling salesperson problem on a complete network with vertices A, B, C, D, E. (The weight of arc DA is 7.)
lines: From A the nearest unvisited vertex is C (4); from C it is E (3); from E it is B (5); from B it is D (6).
Every vertex has now been visited.
Upper bound = 4 + 3 + 5 + 6 = 18.
A different starting vertex might give a better (smaller) upper bound.
spotTheError.explanation: Nearest neighbour for the TSP must produce a complete CYCLE, returning to the start. The tour is A–C–E–B–D–A, so arc DA (7) must be included: upper bound = 4 + 3 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 25. (The 2024 examiner report flagged exactly this slip: 'a path or cycle, not just a sum of arc weights'.)

spotTheError.prompt: A connected planar graph has 7 vertices and 11 edges. Find the number of faces.
lines: Euler's formula states that V + E − F = 2 for a connected planar graph.
Substituting: 7 + 11 − F = 2.
Therefore the graph has 16 faces.
spotTheError.explanation: Euler's formula is V − E + F = 2 (vertices MINUS edges plus faces). Correctly: 7 − 11 + F = 2, so F = 6. Quoting the formula the wrong way round loses everything that follows.

spotTheError.prompt: Activity K has duration 5. It starts at event i and ends at event j, where EET(i) = 8, LET(i) = 10, EET(j) = 15 and LET(j) = 19. Find the total float of K.
lines: Total float = EET(j) − EET(i) − duration.
Total float = 15 − 8 − 5 = 2.
The total float of K is 2.
Since the total float is not zero, K is not a critical activity.
spotTheError.explanation: Total float = LET(j) − EET(i) − duration: the LATEST time of the end event minus the earliest time of the start event minus the duration. Correctly: 19 − 8 − 5 = 6. (K is indeed non-critical, but its float is 6, not 2.)
